# Appendix B: Answers to Review Questions

These are model answers to the review questions at the end of each chapter. They are
deliberately concise: each states the essential points and names the section where the
chapter develops them, so that you can check your own answer against the text and not just
against this page. Where a question asks for your own design, opinion or experience, the
answer shows what a strong response contains; other well-reasoned answers are equally valid.

---

## Chapter 1 — Introduction to Prompt Engineering: Volume II Overview

**1.** Prompt engineering is the systematic practice of designing, refining, evaluating and
maintaining the inputs to a language model so that it reliably produces the outputs a task
requires. Casual use is informed guessing, adjusted until one output looks right;
professional prompt engineering uses a defined methodology, measurable outcomes,
reproducibility, maintainable and versioned artifacts, and an understanding of how the model
works. (Section 1.1)

**2.** A model computes a probability distribution over the next token conditioned on its
entire context, and every token in the prompt is part of that context. Changing one word
changes the conditioning and therefore the distribution, which can tip the model toward a
different role, format, level of hedging or way of reasoning, and early differences compound
as each generated token conditions the next. (Section 1.2)

**3.** Requirements: define the task, audience, constraints, output format and success
criteria. Design: choose patterns and draft the components. Development: write the prompt as
a structured artifact with templates and variable slots. Testing: run it against a
representative test set and measure. Optimization: iterate on the results, using ablation to
find what helps. Deployment: package it as a versioned artifact in the pipeline. Monitoring:
track quality over time, detect drift and re-test when the model changes. (Section 1.5)

**4.** A few outputs that look right are a sample of one person's expectations, not evidence
about the full range of inputs a prompt will meet. Professional work needs reproducible,
measurable results across a representative test set: a prompt that looks right on three
examples can fail on a meaningful share of real traffic, as Chapter 11's opening shows, and
"looks right" gives no basis for comparing versions or detecting regressions. (Sections 1.1,
1.8)

**5.** This question asks for self-assessment, so answers will differ. A strong answer names
one of the five layers (domain knowledge, LLM theory, prompt techniques, evaluation or systems
integration), gives a concrete reason for choosing it, and commits to specific, checkable
actions tied to chapters of this volume: for evaluation, for example, building a 50-case test
set for a real task using Chapters 11 and 13 and reporting its scores. (Section 1.4)

---

## Chapter 2 — Prompt Anatomy: Dissecting Every Component

**1.** A role declaration ("You are a…"); behavioral rules, a numbered list of specific dos and
don'ts; an output specification with the exact format requirements; and a scope definition of
the topics in and out of bounds. (Section 2.2.3)

**2.** Long-context models use information near the beginning and end of the context more
reliably than information in the middle. In a context block, put the most task-critical
content at the beginning or end, never bury essential facts in the middle of long documents,
and keep the block focused so there is less middle to lose things in. (Section 2.3.2)

**3.** Prefill is most valuable when the output must begin with a specific token or structure
and when preamble must be avoided in a strict production format. Two use cases: starting the
response with `{` so the model completes a JSON object instead of writing prose around it, and
starting it with a fixed heading or label so a report follows a required structure. Support
varies by model and is unavailable with extended thinking, and native structured outputs are
stronger still for JSON. (Section 2.6)

**4.** An explicit output trigger is a phrase such as "Begin:", "Output:" or "Answer:" at the
end of the user prompt. It signals the model to stop reading instructions and start producing
the output, and it discourages preamble such as "Sure, I'd be happy to…". (Section 2.5.3)

**5.** The user prompt: end it with an explicit output trigger, and make the format
instruction say that the response must begin directly with the requested output and contain
nothing else. Where the API supports it, prefilling the first characters of the response is a
stronger fix. (Sections 2.5.3, 2.6; Mistake 5)

---

## Chapter 3 — Instruction Design: Engineering Clarity and Specificity

**1.** Specific: the instruction says exactly what the model should do. Measurable: you can
objectively tell whether it was followed. Actionable: the model is able to do what it asks.
Relevant: it serves the task's goal. Terminal: it has a clear stopping point. (Section 3.2)

**2.** A negative instruction names the behavior to avoid without describing the behavior
wanted, so it asks the model to suppress a pattern, a weaker signal than specifying the desired
output directly; research on negated prompts has found that language models handle negation
less reliably than equivalent positive instructions. Rewriting each "do not" as what the model
should do instead gives it a target. (Section 3.6)

**3.** Instructions at the end of a prompt block, closest to where generation begins, tend to
be followed more reliably than those in the middle, and the first instructions also carry
extra weight, while those in the middle of a long list are the most likely to be neglected.
Put the most important rules at the top of the system prompt, restate the one or two most
critical constraints just before the output trigger, and never bury a critical requirement in
the middle of a long list. (Section 3.7)

**4.** One good decomposition: (1) read the document and identify its main topics; (2) extract
the five most important findings or decisions; (3) for each, state its business implication in
one sentence; (4) write a summary of no more than 150 words for an executive audience that
leads with the most important point; (5) list the key points as bullets beneath the summary,
each under 20 words. A strong answer gives each step one verb, a measurable output and an
order. (Section 3.5)

**5.** It is an instruction conflict: the two instructions can require different behavior, so
the model resolves the tension with its own judgment, unpredictably. Resolve it by deciding
what each means for the task, for example "Cover all three risks, in no more than 150 words,"
or by stating which takes precedence, and run a conflict audit on the whole prompt before
deploying. (Section 3.8)

---

## Chapter 4 — Context Design: What to Include and How to Position It

**1.** Models use information at the beginning and end of a long context more reliably than
information in the middle, so content placed in the middle may effectively be ignored. Context
design should place the most critical information at the beginning or end of the context
block, order retrieved documents by relevance, filter out low-relevance material so there is
less to bury, and label sections so the model can locate them. (Sections 4.4, 4.5)

**2.** Define the relevance criterion as a question about what the model needs to know for
this task; audit each candidate document or data element against that question; classify each
as include, summarize to key points, or exclude; and validate the filtered set as a whole,
checking that nothing needed is missing and nothing included adds no value. (Section 4.3.1)

**3.** Prompt injection embeds instructions in user-supplied content, such as a customer note
or retrieved text, in an attempt to override the system prompt. Any two defenses: instruction
anchoring, a clear statement in the system prompt that content in context sections is data and
cannot change the rules; input sanitization; a structured context schema that admits only
validated fields; and isolation labeling that separates user-controlled from system-controlled
context. No single defense is complete, so they are layered. (Section 4.7)

**4.** Without a date the model cannot tell whether information is current, so it may present
an expired policy or price as true and cannot reason about which of two conflicting documents
supersedes the other. Date stamps, with the current date included in the prompt, let it prefer
the newer source and flag stale information. (Section 4.8, Insight 4; Mistake 3)

**5.** A strong answer applies relevance filtering first: score the 15 documents against the
question and drop those that do not bear on it. Then compress what remains, extracting only the
relevant passages from long documents, summarizing tangential ones to key facts, and
restructuring dense prose as tables or lists, until the total fits within 4,000 tokens with
room left for instructions. Finally, order the result with the most relevant material at the
beginning and end, label and date each document, and check answer quality against the
uncompressed version. (Sections 4.3, 4.4, 4.6)

---

## Chapter 5 — Role Prompting: Personas, Expert Roles, and Author Voice

**1.** Any four of the influences the chapter lists: vocabulary selection, the terminology of
the domain; reasoning patterns, the inferential conventions the domain uses; projected
confidence, how certain the output sounds; output structure, how professionals in the domain
organize their communication; and scope boundaries, which questions the role would and would
not take on. A strong answer adds the chapter's caveat: these effects on presentation are
reliable, while the effect on factual accuracy is weak and mixed, so accuracy must come from
context. (Section 5.1)

**2.** A Level 2 role adds a specialization and experience level to the title. A Level 3 role
adds context and behavioral characteristics: the situation the expert is working in, how they
communicate, and how they handle uncertainty. Choose Level 3 when you need a consistent
expert style across many interactions and explicit behavior, such as stating uncertainty, in a
production system. (Section 5.2)

**3.** Persona drift is the gradual return of a model, over a long conversation, from its
specified role to default behavior: generic vocabulary, uniform hedging and conversational
prose. Two techniques: a role reinforcement anchor, a brief role reminder at the start of each
user turn in automated systems, and a system prompt refresh that re-inserts the system prompt
every few turns. A self-check instruction is a third option whose effect varies by model.
(Section 5.5)

**4.** An expert role makes the model sound authoritative and less inclined to hedge, but it
does not supply knowledge, so on questions where the model's knowledge is uncertain or absent
it states wrong answers with more confidence, and those are more likely to be trusted. Every
expert role should include an explicit uncertainty rule: when the model is not confident, or
the answer depends on information it lacks, it must say so and explain what would be needed to
answer reliably. (Sections 5.6.1, 5.6.3)

**5.** Decline: a role that exists to get around safety behavior is the misuse described in
Section 5.6.2, and production systems should filter output regardless of the role. For
legitimate work, suggest a role such as "a security researcher conducting an authorized
penetration test" or "an application-security reviewer," scoped to defensive analysis of
systems the team is authorized to test, with rules to explain vulnerabilities and remediation
and an explicit uncertainty rule. (Section 5.6.2)

---

## Chapter 6 — Few-Shot Learning: Examples as Behavioral Programs

**1.** In-context learning is a model's ability to perform a task from a few input–output
demonstrations placed in its prompt. Nothing about the model changes: the examples condition
the next-token distribution for that one request, and the model infers the pattern, format and
decision boundary they share. Fine-tuning instead updates the model's weights by further
training, so the change persists across requests and needs data, compute and a training run.
(Section 6.1)

**2.** Representativeness: the examples reflect the inputs the model will see in production;
test by asking, for each example, whether it resembles real traffic. Correctness: every output
is exactly what you want; test by having a domain expert review each one. Diversity: the set
covers the range of lengths, styles, topics and difficulty; test by checking whether removing
any one example would leave a gap, and replacing near-duplicates. Clarity: each example
demonstrates the pattern unambiguously; test by showing the pairs, without the task
description, to a colleague and asking whether they can infer the rule. (Section 6.3)

**3.** The examples act as evidence about the label distribution, and models show a
majority-label bias: labels that appear more often in the examples get higher predicted
probability, so three positive examples and one negative push predictions toward positive. A
recency bias compounds it, because the examples nearest the test input have the strongest
influence; if those happen to share a label, that label is favored further. Balance the
classes and interleave them to counter both. (Sections 6.4, 6.5)

**4.** Use dynamic selection when inputs are diverse, the label set is large or formats vary,
so that no small fixed set represents them well, and when you have more good examples than fit
in a prompt. It requires a library of labeled examples, an embedding model to embed the input
and the examples, a vector index or similarity search to retrieve the nearest examples at
runtime, and code that assembles them into the prompt. (Section 6.7)

**5.** Check every example for correctness first and drop any that are wrong or ambiguous.
Then pick for coverage: at least one example per class, keeping the counts balanced, drawn
from the commonest input types, plus one of the edge cases that cause errors; prefer examples
that differ from one another in length and style. Order them interleaved, with the most
representative or hardest example last, and test the chosen set against the remaining 45 as an
evaluation set before adopting it. (Sections 6.3–6.5)

---

## Chapter 7 — Chain-of-Thought Prompting: Engineering Reasoning

**1.** Writing out intermediate steps makes the model spend extra token computation on the
problem before committing to an answer: each step becomes context that conditions the next,
serving as working memory that carries intermediate results forward, and the prompt elicits
the step-by-step patterns of worked solutions in the training data. Without it, the model must
jump to the answer in one prediction, by pattern matching. (Sections 7.1, 7.2)

**2.** Representative difficulty, similar to the target problems; correct reasoning, with every
step factually and logically right; granular decomposition, with one sub-problem per step; and
explicit labeling of each step. (Section 7.4.1)

**3.** Unfaithful reasoning is a plausible-looking chain that does not actually derive the
stated conclusion, so the chain and the answer disagree, or the model reached the answer
another way and wrote the chain afterwards. Detect it by parsing the chain and checking the
final answer against the chain's own conclusion and intermediate results, independently
verifying the answer, and comparing several independently sampled chains. (Section 7.7.1)

**4.** Choose zero-shot CoT when you need a quick improvement with no examples to hand, the
task varies widely, or prompt length matters, since it needs only a trigger phrase. Choose
few-shot CoT when reliability matters and you can invest in demonstrations, because worked
examples control the format and granularity of the reasoning. The trade-off is effort and prompt
length against consistency. For reasoning models, explicit CoT prompts add little. (Sections
7.3, 7.4)

**5.** The model first poses a more general, abstract version of the question, answers it, and
then applies that general answer to the specific case. A non-mathematical example: "Should our
company's employee-of-the-month award go to the person who closed the most sales or to the one
who mentored most new hires?" benefits from first asking "What should a recognition program
reward to support the organization's goals?" (Section 7.6)

---

## Chapter 8 — Structured Prompting: Templates, Frameworks, and XML Architectures

**1.** Role: who the model is. Instructions: what it must do. Steps: how it should approach the
task. End goal: what success looks like. Narrowing: the constraints that apply. (Section 8.2)

**2.** Choose RTF (Role, Task, Format) for simple, single-turn, well-defined tasks where
RISEN's full specification would be excessive, such as "You are a copy editor. Correct the
grammar in the paragraph below. Return only the corrected paragraph." Use RISEN when the task
needs explicit steps and constraints. (Section 8.3)

**3.** Any four: component isolation, so one rule or section can be changed without touching
the others; clearly marked variable slots; parseability, so prompts can be validated, tested and
documented automatically; nesting, for hierarchical requirements; and more generally better
readability, debugging and versioning, because each section can be diffed and attributed.
(Sections 8.1, 8.4.2)

**4.** A variable slot is a marked placeholder in a template, filled with runtime data, such as
`{{customer_message}}`. Documenting the variable schema (name, type, required or optional,
allowed values or length, and an example) tells everyone what may go into each slot, prevents
malformed or oversized inputs, and keeps the template maintainable when someone other than its
author runs it. (Section 8.6)

**5.** Recommend XML-structured prompts built from shared templates, with a consistent tag
naming convention, documented variable schemas, and the prompts stored as versioned artifacts,
for example JSON or YAML records with an ID and version, in version control. At 50 prompts and
three maintainers, consistency and component isolation let people edit one part without
breaking others, and let changes be reviewed, diffed and rolled back; Chapters 17 and 18 extend
this into frameworks and a governed library. (Sections 8.4–8.6)

---

## Chapter 9 — Output Control: Format, Structure, and Length Engineering

**1.** Level 1, a prose instruction ("Return a JSON object"), is the least reliable. Level 2,
a structural instruction with a specific schema in the system prompt, is more reliable. Level 3,
prefill, starting the assistant turn with `{`, is more reliable still. Level 4, constrained
generation through JSON mode or grammar constraints, is the most reliable, and with strict
schema adherence conformance is guaranteed. Production systems should use Level 3 or 4.
(Section 9.2, Table 9.1)

**2.** The output-token limit is a hard cutoff, not a length target: it stops generation
wherever the limit falls, often mid-sentence or mid-structure, and does not make the model plan
a shorter answer. Combine it with explicit length instructions (a count, range or calibrated
examples), and set the limit consistently above the requested length so it acts as a safety
net instead of truncating normal outputs. (Section 9.4)

**3.** Use stop tokens when generation should end at a known delimiter, so that nothing after
it is generated or billed. Production uses include extracting one item from a list by stopping
at the next item's marker, stopping at a section delimiter such as `---`, and requiring a
completion marker such as `[END]` so the output ends cleanly. Choose stop strings that never
occur in normal content. (Section 9.5)

**4.** Parse validation checks that the output parses in the expected format, such as valid
JSON. Schema validation checks that it has the required fields, types and allowed values.
Business-logic validation checks that the values make sense for the application, such as
ranges, consistency and references that exist. Failures trigger a retry and then a fallback.
(Section 9.7)

**5.** Use API-level structured output, JSON mode or strict schema adherence, which constrains
generation itself; prefill the response with `{` where structured output is unavailable; and
reinforce the format at several points (system prompt, immediately before the input, and an
output trigger), possibly with a negative example of the preamble. Add a validation layer that
parses each response and retries on failure, so remaining errors never reach downstream
systems. (Sections 9.3, 9.6, 9.7)

---

## Chapter 10 — Reasoning Strategies: Advanced Multi-Step Inference Techniques

**1.** Compositional reasoning solves a problem by first answering a sequence of simpler
sub-questions, each building on the last. Standard chain-of-thought generates steps linearly
without explicitly decomposing the problem into separately solvable sub-problems, so it can
skip or muddle a needed sub-result; least-to-most prompting adds an explicit decomposition phase
and then solves the sub-problems in order. (Section 10.2)

**2.** Self-consistency samples several independent reasoning chains for the same problem and
takes the majority answer, because correct answers tend to recur more often than any single
incorrect one. A moderately high temperature is used, the original work sampled at about
0.5–0.7 and 0.5–0.9 is a reasonable range to test, because the method needs diverse chains:
at temperature 0 every sample would be the same. (Section 10.3)

**3.** Thought decomposition, defining what a single reasoning step or "thought" is; thought
generation, producing several candidate thoughts at each step; state evaluation, scoring how
promising each candidate is; and a search algorithm, breadth-first or depth-first, over the tree
of thoughts. It is worth the cost for problems with several valid approaches, for planning in
which early decisions matter a great deal, for puzzles that need look-ahead, and where the best
first step is not obvious, when the cost of wrong reasoning justifies extra calls. (Section 10.4)

**4.** Analogical reasoning solves a novel problem by mapping it to a structurally similar,
well-understood problem and transferring that problem's solution approach. For example,
allocating a limited marketing budget across channels with uncertain returns can be framed as a
portfolio-allocation or multi-armed-bandit problem, borrowing diversification and
explore–exploit strategies. (Section 10.5)

**5.** Tree of Thoughts. Choosing 5 of 20 features is exploratory: many combinations are
plausible, early choices constrain later ones, and the best set is not obvious, which matches
the framework's exploratory branch. It is not primarily compositional, so least-to-most is a
poorer fit; self-consistency could be added if the stakes justify sampling several complete
evaluations. A strong answer also notes that the search needs a clear way to evaluate a
candidate set, such as estimated user value against cost. (Section 10.6, Figure 10.3)

---

## Chapter 11 — Prompt Evaluation: Measuring What Matters

**1.** BLEU rewards matching words, not matching meaning, so a correct paraphrase such as "They
pushed the meeting back" scores poorly against "The meeting was postponed"; it correlates poorly
with human judgment on open-ended generation, where many different outputs are good; and it
needs a reference answer, which production traffic does not have. It remains a reasonable
baseline for translation. (Section 11.2.1)

**2.** A strong rubric has three to five distinct dimensions, each with observable descriptions
for every scale point. For example: **Medical accuracy**: 5, every claim consistent with
current clinical guidance; 3, minor imprecision that would not change a decision; 1, at least
one claim that is wrong or unsafe. **Safety and escalation**: 5, recognizes urgent symptoms and
directs the person to emergency care, and states that it is not a substitute for a clinician;
3, appropriate caution but escalation advice vague; 1, misses an urgent condition or gives
advice that could cause harm. **Clarity for a lay reader**: 5, plain language, technical terms
explained, directly answers the question; 3, understandable with effort; 1, jargon-heavy or
does not answer the question. Levels 4 and 2 are defined between these, and the rubric is
tested for inter-annotator agreement before use. (Section 11.4.1, Table 11.2)

**3.** LLM-as-judge uses a language model to score the outputs of another model, or itself,
against a rubric, so that evaluation scales to volumes people cannot review. Principles: use a
stronger model as the judge; give it an explicit rubric with the same dimensions and scale you
would give human raters; require structured output with per-dimension scores and reasoning;
prefer pairwise comparison where possible, controlling position bias; and calibrate it against
human judgments on 50–100 items before relying on it. (Section 11.5.1)

**4.** In pairwise comparison, judges tend to prefer the response in a particular position,
often the first, regardless of quality. Test by evaluating each pair twice with the order
swapped and measuring how often the verdict follows the position instead of the content.
Mitigate by randomizing order, or by running both orders and counting only consistent verdicts,
or averaging them. (Section 11.5; Mistake 4)

**5.** Programmatic checks, such as parsing JSON, validating a schema, running code or matching
a known label, are fast, cheap, deterministic and catch the failures that hurt most: an output
that does not parse is an outage, however well written. Running them first filters out
structural failures before slower, costlier and noisier semantic metrics and judges are spent
on outputs that have already failed. (Section 11.3.1)

---

## Chapter 12 — Prompt Optimization: Manual Iteration and Automatic Methods

**1.** With only API access to a model, the prompt is discrete text and the quality metric is
not differentiable with respect to it, so there is no gradient to follow; each candidate must
be evaluated with model calls. (Soft prompt tuning, which learns continuous embeddings by
gradient descent, needs the model's weights and is a different technique.) The alternatives
are gradient-free: structured manual iteration, LLM-generated candidates (APE), optimization by
prompting with a history of scored candidates (OPRO), and declarative optimization of
instructions and demonstrations (DSPy). (Sections 12.1, 12.3–12.5)

**2.** Changing one component per iteration makes each change attributable: if quality moves,
you know which change moved it. Several simultaneous changes confound one another, so you
cannot tell which helped, which hurt or which interacted, and you cannot safely undo or keep
any of them. It builds a reliable model of what works and often converges faster than
multi-variable guessing. (Section 12.2.1)

**3.** Define the task with a small labeled dataset; use an LLM to generate candidate
instructions from the input–output examples; evaluate every candidate on the labeled dataset
with the quality metric and select the best; then iterate, generating variations of the best
instructions aimed at the remaining failures. (Section 12.3.1)

**4.** DSPy optimizes what happens inside a prompt pipeline the programmer has written: the
few-shot demonstrations each module uses, the instruction text, and, with some optimizers, the
model's weights through fine-tuning on bootstrapped examples. APE searches only for the text of
a single instruction; DSPy optimizes whole multi-module programs declared by signatures, with
the module composition chosen by the programmer. (Sections 12.3, 12.5)

**5.** Split the 200 examples into a development set for optimizing and a held-out test set that
is never used until the end, for example 150 and 50. Categorize the failures on the development
set by type, and iterate manually one change at a time on the largest failure category,
re-scoring after each change. If manual progress stalls, run an automatic method such as APE,
or DSPy to optimize instructions and few-shot examples, against the development set. Confirm the
final prompt on the held-out set to check for overfitting, and stop when gains diminish.
(Sections 12.2, 12.6; Insight 4)

---

## Chapter 13 — Prompt Testing: Regression, Edge Cases, and A/B Testing

**1.** Golden-set tests, 20–50 representative cases that define core functionality and must
pass at 100%; regression tests, accumulated from every bug found and fixed so that it cannot
return; edge-case tests, unusual but valid inputs at the boundaries of the task; and
adversarial tests, attempts to break the prompt through injection, jailbreaks, gibberish or
out-of-scope requests. (Section 13.2)

**2.** Never fix a prompt bug without adding the input that triggered it to the regression
suite. It matters because prompt changes made for other reasons can silently reintroduce old
bugs; the regression suite records every known failure in a form that runs on every change, as
the weekend-delivery test that caught Wren's reintroduced bug shows. (Section 13.2.2)

**3.** Checking results repeatedly and stopping as soon as they look significant inflates the
false-positive rate: with each look there is another chance for random variation to cross the
threshold. Significance tests assume the sample size was fixed in advance, so decide it with a
power calculation and evaluate once it is reached. (Section 13.5.2)

**4.** They are thresholds, defined before the rollout begins, that trigger a rollback
automatically when breached, for example an error rate above twice the baseline, P95 latency
above 1.5 times the baseline, a drop in the output-validation pass rate, or cost per request
above a limit. Define them from the stable version's measured baseline, include quality and
cost as well as errors, and give each an owner and an automated action. (Sections 13.6; Volume
IV, Section 5.10)

**5.** A strong answer starts small and slow because of the stakes. For example: shadow-test the
new prompt on recent queries; then 1% of traffic for 48 hours with every response sampled for
clinician review; then 5% for 48 hours; then 25% for a few days; then 100%. Rollback criteria,
fixed in advance: any response flagged as clinically unsafe; a drop in the safety or accuracy
score against the baseline beyond normal variation; a rise in refusals or escalations beyond
normal variation; an error-rate or latency breach. Monitor the same metrics as the test suite
plus clinical review findings, and require sign-off from the accountable owner before each
ramp. (Section 13.6)

---

## Chapter 14 — Prompt Debugging: Systematic Failure Diagnosis

**1.** Reproduce the failure on the known failing input, running it several times and recording
how often it fails, because model output varies. Reproduction must come first because without a
reliable failure, and its baseline rate, you cannot tell whether a change fixed the problem or
the failure simply did not occur that time. (Section 14.2.1)

**2.** Ablation removes or changes one component at a time to discover which one causes a
failure when you do not yet know. Contrastive prompting compares two nearly identical prompts
that differ in exactly one element, to test a specific hypothesis about what causes it. Use
ablation for open-ended diagnosis and contrastive prompting when you already suspect the cause,
since it tests that suspicion in one step. (Sections 14.2, 14.3; Insight 4)

**3.** Any five of the "always log" fields: prompt ID and version; the full input, sanitized of
personal data; model and version; temperature, output-token limit and stop tokens; the full raw
output; latency; and token counts for input and output. (Section 14.4.1)

**4.** Two instructions in the prompt can require different behavior for some inputs, so the
model sometimes follows one and sometimes the other. Diagnose it by noticing inconsistent
behavior on similar inputs and running a conflict audit, asking for each pair of instructions
whether they can ever require different behavior. Resolve it by making the conflict explicit:
state which instruction takes precedence, or rewrite them so that both can be satisfied.
(Section 14.5.3)

**5.** Reproduce the failures on a sample of long and short inputs to confirm the length effect
and its rate. Classify the failures (truncation, preamble, drifting format, wrong schema) from
the logs, grouping failures by input length and template. Check whether the output-token limit
truncates longer responses. Then test the format-drift hypothesis contrastively, for example by
restating the format requirement just before the output trigger or adding prefill or structured
output, and ablate other components if that does not explain it. Add the failing long inputs to
the regression suite once fixed. (Sections 14.2–14.5)

---

## Chapter 15 — Prompt Patterns: A Catalog of Proven Approaches

**1.** The same problems recur across prompts, and the same classes of solution keep working.
Documenting them as named patterns, with intent, motivation, structure, example and when to use
them, transfers expertise, gives teams a shared vocabulary for comparing approaches, and saves
practitioners from reinventing solutions, as Wren's three different ways of asking for a missing
tracking number showed. (Introduction; Section 15.1)

**2.** The model asks the user for the information it needs instead of receiving everything up
front, guiding the gathering of information. It is most valuable when users do not know what the
model needs or the required inputs are complex, as in consulting-style interactions or content
that depends on personal details; for simple tasks a template with a structured input form is
lighter. (Section 15.7)

**3.** Choose it when the boundary between provided context and the model's own knowledge must
be explicit: in RAG pipelines and document analysis, when answers must come only from the
supplied material, when training knowledge may be outdated or conflict with it, or when the
model should state that the context does not contain the answer. Without explicit scoping,
models blend training knowledge with context unpredictably. (Section 15.4)

**4.** A strong answer fixes the output structure with a template and requires a citation for
every factual statement, for example:

```text
You are a technical writer documenting our REST API from the source material provided.

Use only the information in <source>. After every factual statement, cite its source in
brackets, for example [api-spec, §2.1]. If the source does not cover something the
template requires, write "Not specified in source" instead of inferring it.

Fill this template exactly:

## Endpoint: {name}
**Purpose:** one sentence. [citation]
**Request:** method, path and parameters as a table. [citation]
**Response:** fields and types as a table. [citation]
**Errors:** each error code and its meaning. [citation]
**Example:** one request and response, taken from the source. [citation]

<source>
{{api_spec_excerpt}}
</source>

Begin:
```

(Sections 15.3, 15.10, 15.11)

**5.** A reasonable choice is Context Manager, Template and Fact Attribution. Context Manager
restricts answers to the contract text supplied; Template fixes the structure of each analysis
(parties, obligations, termination, liability, risks) so outputs are consistent and machine
readable; and Fact Attribution requires every statement to cite the clause it comes from, so a
reviewer can verify it. Alternatives such as Cognitive Verifier, for breaking a complex question
into sub-questions, are defensible with a reason. Whatever the combination, test it against a
single-pattern baseline before adopting it. (Sections 15.4, 15.3, 15.10; Mistake 3)

---

## Chapter 16 — Prompt Anti-Patterns: What Not to Do and Why

**1.** Negative instructions name the behavior to avoid without describing what to do instead,
and models follow them less reliably than positive instructions; strongly learned behavior often
overrides a "do not." The reliable alternative is to rewrite each negation as a positive
specification of the wanted behavior, for example "Use plain words a non-specialist would
understand" in place of "Don't use jargon." (Section 16.5; Chapter 3, Section 3.6)

**2.** RLHF rewards outputs people prefer, and people often prefer agreement, so models tend to
validate the user's assumptions and present the positive case even when it is wrong. Counter it
with explicit instructions for honest evaluation: ask for the strongest weaknesses and risks as
well as the strengths, give permission to disagree, and require evidence for each claim. Test for
it directly by presenting a clearly flawed idea and checking whether the model pushes back.
(Section 16.6; Insight 3)

**3.** Prompt bloat is the growth of a prompt over time as fixes are added on top of fixes,
producing a long document full of contradictions, redundancies and obsolete rules, such as Wren's
thirty-one rules with two that contradicted each other. Prevent it with periodic audits that
consolidate, deduplicate and remove outdated instructions, a single owner, and the versioning
and maintenance practices of Chapters 17 and 18. (Section 16.9)

**4.** Context overload is supplying far more context than the task needs, so irrelevant material
dilutes the relevant and the model misses critical information or answers generically. It
interacts with the lost-in-the-middle effect, because a large block of context has a long middle
where important information is used least reliably. The remedy is relevance filtering,
summarizing tangential material and extracting key passages. (Section 16.8)

**5.** The prompt shows several anti-patterns. A vague role: "a helpful assistant" constrains
nothing. Negation abuse: two of its rules are "Don't." Conflicting instructions: "Don't be too
brief" and "Always explain everything" pull against "Be clear," with no stopping point, and
"Don't use technical words" conflicts with helping with code. An ambiguous task with no audience,
output format or length. A strong rewrite specifies the role and audience ("an assistant helping
beginner Python programmers"), states positive rules with measurable limits ("explain each
concept in plain language, define any technical term you must use, keep answers under 250 words
unless the user asks for more, include a short code example"), and says what to do when a
question is out of scope. (Sections 16.2, 16.5, 16.7, 16.10, 16.11)

---

## Chapter 17 — Reusable Prompt Frameworks

**1.** A template is a parametric prompt string with variable slots. A framework is a governed,
reusable structure for a whole class of prompts: it adds behavioral contracts (output format,
certainty signaling, fallback behavior), composability (assembly from or extension of other
frameworks) and governance (version, owner, approval history and deprecation path). For example,
a framework provides an invariant header shared by every prompt built from it, an output
contract validated with a JSON Schema, and adapter hooks for specialization, none of which a
plain template has. (Sections 17.1, 17.3)

**2.** The invariant header is shared by every prompt and application built on the framework.
Real data there, such as customer names, configurations or URLs, is exposed to every consumer
and every model call that uses the framework, including in other contexts, which is a data leak,
and it ties the framework to one situation so it cannot be reused safely. All real data must
flow through parameterized slots at runtime; the header contains only structural and behavioral
text. (Section 17.11, Anti-Pattern 3)

**3.** Any well-argued example. Processing an insurance or damage claim, for instance, can be
split into extracting the claim fields from the email, classifying the claim type, checking the
evidence against the policy and drafting a decision summary. Each stage has its own focused
prompt, input contract and output contract, so each can be tested, validated and improved
separately, and intermediate results can be checked. One prompt doing everything is harder to
debug, mixes concerns that compete for attention, fails less transparently, and cannot route
part of the work to cheaper models or to people. (Section 17.7)

**4.** Adding new required output fields changes the output contract, so it is a breaking change
and takes a MAJOR increment, for example from 1.x.x to 2.0.0. Consumers parsing the old schema
may fail, or must start handling the new fields. Announce the change to every consuming
application with a migration note describing the new fields and their meaning, keep the old
version available, and deprecate it through the protocol of announcement, a warning period and
archiving instead of deleting it; applications must pin explicit versions so that none changes
silently. (Section 17.10)

**5.** The likeliest cause is an untested framework: an evaluation framework deployed without a
test suite and never calibrated against human judgment, so nothing detects that its scores have
lost their meaning. A judge model's verbosity or self-preference bias, or a rubric with vague
scale points, would produce exactly this inflation. Diagnose it by running the framework on a
calibration set of responses with known human ratings, including clearly poor ones, and
measuring agreement. Fix it by anchoring each scale point with observable criteria and examples,
using a judge from a different model family, adding regression tests with known-bad outputs, and
recalibrating after every change. (Sections 17.8, 17.11 Anti-Pattern 5; Chapter 11, Section
11.5)

**6.** Use the Template Pattern alone when the main need is a consistent, parseable output
structure, such as extracting fields into a fixed schema. Use the Role Pattern alone when the
main need is a domain's vocabulary, conventions and tone, such as drafting advice in a
particular professional voice. Compose them when both matter: for example, a security-review
prompt in which a security-reviewer role shapes how findings are judged and explained, while a
template fixes the finding format (location, severity, evidence, remediation) so findings can be
merged and tracked. The role shapes presentation; accurate knowledge still comes from context.
(Sections 17.5, 17.6)

---

## Chapter 18 — Professional Prompt Libraries

**1.** The storage layer holds the prompt files and their metadata; the registry layer indexes
and searches them; the API layer serves prompts to applications, enforcing access control and
hiding storage; the test layer runs automated tests on every change; and the governance layer
handles review, approval and access control. Without storage there is no single source of
truth. Without a registry prompts cannot be found, so they are duplicated. Without an API,
applications read files directly and bypass access control and telemetry. Without tests, changes
cause silent regressions. Without governance, undiscussed changes break dependents and sensitive
prompts leak. (Section 18.2)

**2.** A schema test checks that the output parses and is structurally correct, and is most
likely to catch changes to the format instructions, the output contract or the model. A
behavioral test checks that known inputs produce the expected values, and catches changes to
instructions, examples or model behavior. A regression test checks that a fixed set of
input–output pairs stays stable across versions, testing properties instead of exact strings,
and catches unintended side effects of any edit, including wording changes meant to be
harmless. (Section 18.5)

**3.** Prompts are part of an application's behavior, so changing them is changing code. First
scenario: an edit to one prompt alters its output format, a downstream parser breaks in
production, and without history nobody can identify the change or roll it back. Second
scenario: two teams edit the same prompt, one change silently removes a rule the other depended
on, as in Chapter 8's lost refund cap, and without versions and diffs the regression cannot be
traced. Version control adds history, review through pull requests, tested releases, pinned
versions per application and instant rollback. (Section 18.4)

**4.** Every prompt has exactly one owner, a named team or person accountable for it. The owner
reviews all proposed changes, is responsible for the prompt's test suite, is the first point of
contact for production issues, and carries out the deprecation protocol when the prompt is
retired. A general contributor may propose changes, but approval, quality and accountability
rest with the owner. (Section 18.7)

**5.** A strong answer includes, for each prompt: its ID and version, with full version
history and the date each version was in production; its owner; the purpose and the system or
use case it serves; the deployment status and which applications or services use it; the model
and model version it runs on; the risk classification of the system it belongs to, under the AI
Act's tiers; the reviewer and approval date of each version; links to its tests and evaluation
results; its data-handling notes, for example whether personal data passes through it; and its
deprecation status. An export of these records must reconstruct which prompt was live where and
when. This is engineering guidance; counsel should confirm what the regulation requires.
(Sections 18.3, 18.7; Volume IV, Chapter 12)

**6.** A monorepo keeps prompts with the applications that use them; it is simplest and suits a
small organization with few teams, at the cost of coarse access control. A dedicated library
repository, consumed as a package or submodule, gives precise access control and independent
versioning; it suits several teams sharing prompts, at the cost of a release process. A registry
service serves prompts through an API at runtime and supports the most sophisticated governance
and telemetry; it suits large organizations with many consumers and strong audit needs, at the
cost of operating another service. (Section 18.8)

---

## Chapter 19 — Review Boards and Critique Boards

**1.** A language model generates one token at a time, each conditioned on everything already
written. When it writes the second "expert," the first expert's opinion is already part of its
input, so the second is anchored on it instead of formed independently. The whole panel is also
one sample from the model's output distribution, and the request for consensus tells it to
resolve disagreement before you see it. Independence requires separate calls with separate
contexts. (Section 19.3)

**2.** For example: "You are a contract analyst. Your one question: does every factual statement
in this summary match the contract? Ignore style, formatting and the summary's choice of what to
include; report only statements that conflict with or are not supported by the contract. For
each finding, quote the summary sentence and the contract clause (section number and text) that
contradicts it or is missing. Return a JSON list of findings, each with `location`, `severity`
(critical, major or minor), `evidence` and `confidence`. If you find no factual errors, return an
empty list; that is a valid result." (Section 19.4)

**3.** Synthesis merges the two reports on the same line into one finding, keeping both
severities and reporting the severity dispute explicitly, because the disagreement suggests the
impact depends on an assumption one reviewer made. The third finding is reported in full and
marked as raised by a single reviewer, never dropped for lack of agreement, since catching what
others miss is the point of independence. Before acting on either, verify each against the
artifact: reproduce the problem or check the cited line, and record rejected findings with the
reason. (Section 19.6)

**4.** Any two from Section 19.9: the board is eight model calls with different instructions,
not eight experts, so "approved by eight expert reviewers" overstates the process and invites
false confidence; the reviewers share the blind spots of the models they run on, because
independent contexts are not independent judgment; reviewers instructed to criticize produce
plausible objections that must be verified, not counted, so "approved" hides whether findings
were checked; and running eight roles on every pull request may cost more than the risk
justifies, since board size should follow the stakes. (Section 19.9)

**5.** The record should contain all three verdicts with their conditions, the evidence and
assumptions behind each, the dissenting DO NOT BUILD verdict and its reasons, the decision to
proceed and who made it, and the fact that one condition was not met, with the reason and any
accepted risk. It matters because a board takes no vote and the accountable person decides; if
the project later fails for the reason the dissenter or the unmet condition identified, the
record lets the organization learn from it instead of re-arguing it. (Section 19.7)

**6.** The one-off data-cleaning script needs no board: its consequences are small, and a quick
self-check and tests are enough. The customer-facing refund policy warrants a three-role board,
for example correctness, policy and compliance, and a customer-impact or red-team role, because
errors affect customers and the business directly. The loan-approval feature warrants a larger
board, adding roles such as fairness, legal and regulatory, security and model-risk, and a
Critique Board on whether to build it, because its decisions are high-stakes, regulated and hard
to reverse. Board size follows the stakes. (Sections 19.5.2, 19.8.2)

---

## Chapter 20 — Volume II Capstone Project: Prompt Engineering Workflow

**1.** The weighted total assumes that a higher score is better on every dimension. Because
accuracy risk is defined so that 5 means no risky claims, the evaluator must apply that
definition consistently; if a component treated the dimension the other way round, as a measure
of risk where higher is worse, responses with high-risk claims would raise the weighted total
and could pass the quality gate. The scoring rules are part of the output contract and must be
defined, documented and tested. (Section 20.5)

**2.** The threshold should reflect the cost of an automated mistake against the cost of human
handling, the classifier's measured calibration (how often a stated confidence is right), the
capacity of the human queue, and the risk of each ticket category. A threshold of 0.70 automates
more tickets and loads the human queue less, but lets more misclassifications through; 0.95
sends far more tickets to people, raising cost and response time, but makes fewer automated
errors. Set it from measured precision at each threshold on a validation set, possibly
differently per category. (Sections 20.3, 20.4)

**3.** For example: if the Classifier's output had no defined schema and it returned the
category as free text ("Probably order status") or omitted `confidence`, the routing logic and
the Response Generator, which select a template by category and route on confidence, would fail
or misroute tickets. Defining the JSON schema of each stage's output (Classifier, Response
Generator and Evaluator) before writing any prompt, and validating every output against it,
means each stage receives exactly the fields and types it expects, and a malformed output is
caught at the boundary instead of failing downstream. (Sections 20.4, 20.9)

**4.** No. A fixed 0.05 difference says nothing about whether the difference is larger than
random variation. A rigorous decision needs the sample size and how it was chosen (a power
analysis for the minimum effect worth detecting), the variance of the scores, a significance
test or confidence interval for the difference, a significance level fixed in advance,
guardrail metrics that must not regress, and results across segments. (Section 20.7; Chapter
13, Section 13.5)

**5.** The Operations and Maintenance Guide, because the operations team must keep the system
working without its builders: it tells them what to monitor, when to act, how to change prompts
safely and what to do in an incident. Useful additions beyond Section 20.8's list: an inventory
of models and pinned versions with the procedure for upgrades; cost budgets and alert
thresholds; a runbook for each alert; a rollback procedure with commands; contacts and owners;
how to add a new ticket category; and how to refresh evaluation sets. (Section 20.8)

**6.** Automated evaluation is consistent, cheap, fast and scalable, so it can score every change
and much of production traffic and catch regressions quickly. Only human evaluation reliably
judges subtle qualities such as whether an answer actually helps, whether its tone suits an
upset customer and whether a plausible claim is in fact true, and it is needed to calibrate the
automated judge. A hybrid runs automated checks and a calibrated judge on all or most traffic,
samples a smaller share for human review, sends flagged low-confidence or low-score cases to
people, and uses the human ratings to recalibrate the judge regularly. (Sections 20.5, 20.9;
Chapter 11)
